title: Code
text:
The code that built the database is in the authors’ repository material-contracts: R and Quarto runbooks with the Python extractors and classifiers they call. It is the working repository of the paper, not a packaged replication. The paper’s Stata code has a page of its own.
Two tools of the work have repositories of their own:

title: Code
text:
What needs WRDS
Compustat is licensed and not published. EstiSample marks the attachments in the paper’s estimation sample, which needs a Compustat match on CIK and the filing date, DateFiled; SampleStepCode and SampleStepDesc record the step of the sample selection at which an attachment leaves the sample. Rebuilding the match needs a WRDS subscription; the code is in material-contracts. Neither the database nor any example on this site needs WRDS.

title: The methods
text: Every example on this page reads the sample in sample/: 214 rows of the contracts table. Of these, 180 are labelled contracts, 15 from each of the 12 detailed categories; 3 are attachments the text screen rejected; and 31 are the registrant copies of 3 attachments whose filing names more than one registrant. The sample shows how the files work, not what the corpus looks like.

title: The methods
text:
Classification
Each contract carries three labels, each from a fine-tuned Legal-BERT model (nlpaueb/legal-bert-base-uncased) of its own: a detailed category out of 12, a broad category out of 7, and whether the document is an original contract or an amendment. A model reads the first 256 or the first 512 tokens of a document and ignores the rest. Each task was trained at both lengths, which makes the 6 models of the classifiers part.
The paper’s contract type is Class, the detailed category from the model ClassDetailed_L256, and its broad type is ClassRollup, the roll-up of Class to the broad categories. ClassBroad comes from an additional model trained on the broad labels directly; where it differs from the roll-up, HierConsistent is FALSE.
Cross-validation over five folds of the labelled contracts selected a configuration for each task; for the broad task it selected the 512-token model. The published labels come from the 256-token models in all three tasks.
The detailed categories and the broad category each rolls up to, as the contracts table publishes them:

contracts <- arrow::read_parquet("sample/core/Contracts.parquet")

contracts |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    ClassRollup,  # the broad parent the paper uses
    Class         # the detailed category under it
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(
    ClassRollup,  # parents in alphabetical order
    Class         # and their children below them
  )

Read this agreement as a check that the files fit together, not as accuracy. The labelled sample is the training data of the published models: every document above was among those they were fitted on. Accuracy on documents a model has not seen comes from the cross-validation over the folds, not from this comparison.

Applying a model to your own documents
The classifiers part holds the 6 models as zip archives, one per task and context length. Beside them, models_index.csv maps each archive to the folder it unpacks to; its LabelledPublished marks the models whose output is published, and Selected and MacroF1 the configuration cross-validation chose for each task. deployed.parquet is the record of that selection; it lists the broad model at 512 tokens. README.md in the same folder is the usage guide: it holds the code that applies a model and three rules for reproducing a published column. The input is TextRaw from the documents part, the context length is the one in the archive’s name, and the label mapping comes from the model.

title: The methods
text:
The keyword classifier
Beside each transformer label the contracts table carries a label from a keyword classifier, which its codebook calls an independent second instrument. The core part publishes its lexicon as KeywordTerms.parquet: 160 rows, one per task, category and term, with Task naming the task (ClassDetailed, ClassBroad or AmendType). Term is the keyword, one to three lower-case words searched in the first 256 words of a document. Precision is the share of the labelled documents containing it that belong to its category, and Power, the term’s strength, is the lower bound of the Wilson interval of that precision. The codebook lists the other columns.
The package publishes the terms and the labels they gave; the code that finds a term in a text is in the pipeline (see the Code page). In the contracts table the keyword label of the detailed task is KwClassDetailed, with the keyword that decided it in KwClassDetailedTerm and its Power in KwClassDetailedPower; the label is missing where no keyword applied or two categories tied. The broad task has the same three columns. ClassDetailedFlag and ClassBroadFlag say whether the keyword label confirmed the transformer, contradicted it, or left it unchecked by giving no category. For the amendment task KwAmendType is Amended where an amendment term applies and Original otherwise. The lexicon also lists 12 terms for Original, which that rule does not use.

Worked example
Every row the keyword classifier labelled in the detailed or broad task records the term that decided the label. The terms behind one category:

contracts |>
  dplyr::filter(KwClassDetailed == "Leases") |>
  dplyr::count(
    KwClassDetailedTerm,   # the term that decided the label
    KwClassDetailedPower,  # its Power in the lexicon
    name = "Rows"          # how many rows of the sample it labelled
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(KwClassDetailedPower))

title: The methods
text:
Extraction
The organisation candidates come from LexNLP 2.3.0, run inside the container image of the extraction image part; places, dates, law clauses and redaction markers come from the pipeline’s own extractors. Rules written in R, part of the pipeline, decide which candidates become spans: they match organisations to the registrant and give each party a role, attach places to parties, read the jurisdiction a law clause names, and place each date relative to the filing date. lexnlp/README.md in the extraction image part says how to load and run the image. It is built for linux/arm64; on an Intel or AMD machine Docker runs it under emulation.







Span file
One row per




org_mentions
mention of a party; one row without a span for a contract with none


places_geo
place named, attached to a party or not


law_clauses
law clause


date_spans
date that could be read


term_spans
stated period, or a clause stating the contract has no fixed length


redact_spans
redaction or omission marker



Beside each span the files keep what the rules read: whether a place was attached to a party, whether a date falls before or after the filing, whether a period is left open, whether a marker withholds text. From spans to variables turns one span file into a column of the contracts table.

The span files of the sample
Each span file holds one row per entity found, keyed on the document and located by its offsets into the text (see the data page). Counted per document:

span_files <- list.files(
  "sample/spans",           # every span file of the sample
  pattern = "\\.parquet$",  # the codebook beside them is not a span file
  full.names = TRUE         # read_parquet needs the path, not the name
)
names(span_files) <- sub(
  "\\.parquet$",        # the file extension
  "",                   # dropped, so the name is the kind of span
  basename(span_files)  # the file names without their folder
)
spans <- lapply(
  span_files,          # one path per kind of span
  arrow::read_parquet  # each file read whole: the sample is small
)


per_document <- function(kind) {
  start <- grep(
    "Start$",              # the first ...Start column is the span's own start
    names(spans[[kind]]),  # the columns of this span file
    value = TRUE           # the name rather than its position
  )[1]
  spans[[kind]] |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data[[start]])) |>
    dplyr::count(
      DocID,         # one count per document
      name = "Rows"  # the rows of this kind in the document
    ) |>
    dplyr::summarise(
      Kind = kind,                   # the span file
      Documents = dplyr::n(),        # documents with at least one span
      Spans = sum(Rows),             # spans in all
      Median = stats::median(Rows),  # spans in the typical document
      Max = max(Rows)                # spans in the busiest document
    )
}

names(spans) |>
  lapply(per_document) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()

title: The methods
text:
From spans to variables
TermYears in the contracts table is the longest term the contract states, in years. A contract can state several periods, and term_spans keeps every one of them, with the period in years (TermYears), the phrasing that matched (TermKind) and whether the clause states the contract has no fixed length (IsOpen). The periods with a length:

terms <- arrow::read_parquet("sample/spans/term_spans.parquet")

candidates <- terms |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(TermYears),  # the phrase parsed into a length
    !IsOpen             # an open-ended period has no length to compare
  )

candidates |>
  dplyr::count(
    TermKind,           # the phrase the period came from
    name = "Spans"      # candidates of that kind in the sample
  )





TermKind
Spans

The published rule, recomputed from the spans: the longest of these periods in each contract, against the published column.

per_contract <- candidates |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    LongestStated = max(TermYears),  # the published rule
    Candidates = dplyr::n(),         # periods to choose among
    .by = DocID                      # one value per contract
  ) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    dplyr::select(  # the published column beside the recomputed one
      contracts,    # one row per contract
      DocID,        # the contract
      TermYears     # the published term in years
    ),
    by = "DocID"  # the span files are keyed on the same document
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(TermYears))  # contracts for which a term was published

term_check <- per_contract |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Contracts = dplyr::n(),                   # contracts with a candidate period
    SeveralCandidates = sum(Candidates > 1),  # contracts that state more than one period
    PublishedRuleMatches = sum(dplyr::near(   # contracts the recomputed rule reproduces
      LongestStated,  # the published rule, recomputed
      TermYears       # the published column
    ))
  )

The published column is one rule over the spans. PeriodKind records what each period governs, from the word before it; its codebook adds: “Descriptive only; no variable uses it.” A study that wants the agreement’s own term rather than the longest stated period filters on it and writes its rule in a line.
The span files are keyed on the primary copy of each attachment; HashDocument in the contracts table reaches the other registrant copies.

title: The analysis of material contracts
text: This site publishes the data and the methods of the paper below. The data package holds the material contracts, Exhibit 10 to a filing, that registrants filed with the SEC with forms 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, 20-F, S-1, S-4, F-1 and F-4 and their amendments between 1999 and 2024: 1,462,939 registrant copies of these attachments, classified by type, with the parties, places, law clauses, dates, terms and redactions extracted from their text, and the documents themselves. The paper’s sample starts in 2001.

title: The analysis of material contracts
text:
Four ways in

Data. What each part of the data package holds, the tables and their columns, and three things to know before counting anything.
Methods. How the contracts were classified and their entities extracted, and how to turn the published spans into variables of your own, each with an example on the sample.
Stata. Where the paper’s Stata code will be published, what it needs, and how to read the tables and slice a span in Stata.
Code. Where the code that built the database is, and what needs a WRDS subscription.

Every R example on this site runs, from the root of a clone of the site’s repository, on the sample in its sample/ folder: 15 labelled contracts from each of the 12 detailed categories, 3 rejected attachments and all 31 registrant copies of 3 attachments whose filing names several registrants.

section: The paper and how to cite it
text:
The paper and how to cite it
Ann-Kristin Grosskopf, Victor Sehn and Matthias Uckert. The analysis of material contracts: Use of SEC contractual data in accounting research (under review).
Please cite the paper, and the data package with its version, v1.0.0. The tables and span files are licensed under CC BY 4.0 and the classifiers under CC BY-SA 4.0; the data page says what applies to the documents and the extraction image. Questions and requests to remove material go to m.uckert@uva.nl.

title: The data
text:
The data package v1.0.0 comes in 5 parts: 123 files besides the checksum manifest, 49.5 GB in all, the parts below and a README at the root of the package. Each part is a folder that can be downloaded on its own. The parts are shared from Google Drive, each with its own download link.
Every example on this site reads the sample in sample/ of the site’s repository. It holds 180 contracts of the labelled sample, 15 from each of the 12 detailed categories, plus 3 attachments the text screen rejected and all 31 registrant copies of 3 attachments filed by several registrants, so that the checks below have something to show: 214 rows in all, with the rows every table and span file holds for them. To run an example, clone the repository and run the code from its root. The examples need the R packages arrow, dplyr, stringi and tibble; none needs the data package.

title: The data
text:
The parts

The database
One row per registrant copy of an Exhibit 10 attachment with its filing, classification and content variables, the announcement, place, term and confidential treatment tables beside it, the codebooks, the contract index, the labelled sample and the keyword terms.

424 MB in 16 files
Published: download



Entity spans
The entity spans the rules kept, with their position in the document and the properties the rules read: organisation mentions, places, governing-law clauses, dates, terms and redaction marks.

1.1 GB in 7 files
Published: download



The documents
The retrieved documents themselves, as filed and as text: Exhibit 10 attachments, the current reports (8-K and 8-K/A) that announced a material agreement, and the confidential treatment orders, split by type and filing year.

45.3 GB in 86 files

The classifiers

title: The data
text:
Getting a part
Each part above links to its own folder; the whole package has a link of its own. At the root of the package are a README.md and a MANIFEST.sha256, which lists every file with its SHA-256 checksum. Google Drive may deliver a large folder as several zip files; unpack them into one folder, with MANIFEST.sha256 at its root, before checking. From that folder (macOS, Linux), the first line checks the whole package and the second only the parts its pattern names, here core and spans:
shasum -a 256 -c MANIFEST.sha256
grep -E '  (core|spans)/' MANIFEST.sha256 | shasum -a 256 -c

title: The data
text:
Reading the files
The tables are parquet files. The package’s README reads them as follows:

R: arrow::read_parquet("core/Contracts.parquet")
Python: pandas.read_parquet("core/Contracts.parquet")
SQL: duckdb -c "SELECT count(*) FROM 'core/Contracts.parquet'"

No .dta files are published; the Stata page says how to read the tables in Stata.
The sample keeps the package’s folders, file names and columns, so an example moves to the package by replacing sample/ with the root of the package. The documents are the exception. The sample keeps them in one file, text/exhibit10/exhibit10_sample.parquet, where the package has one file per type and filing year, text/<type>/<type>_<year>.parquet. The sample holds Exhibit 10 attachments only, without the HTML column, the document as retrieved from EDGAR. It carries no contract index, no models and no extraction image.
A file too large for memory is opened lazily and filtered before it is collected:

exhibits <- arrow::open_dataset("sample/text/exhibit10")  # a folder of parquet files, opened as one table
wanted <- arrow::read_parquet(
  "sample/core/Contracts.parquet",  # the contracts table
  col_select = "DocID"              # only the key is needed here
)$DocID[1]                          # one document of the sample

exhibits |>
  dplyr::filter(DocID %in% wanted) |>  # the documents a study needs
  dplyr::select(
    DocID,  # the document
    YQ,     # its filing year and quarter
    DocExt  # its file type as filed
  ) |>
  dplyr::collect()  # the rows are read here

title: The data
section: The tables of the core part
text:
The tables of the core part
The core part holds the tables below with their codebooks, the contract index, the labelled sample and the keyword terms. The meanings shown are the codebook’s own.

Contracts
One row per registrant copy of an Exhibit 10 attachment: 1,462,939 rows, of which the sample holds 214. The filing, the classification and the content variables of the contract sit side by side; below are its keys, the filing, the rejection and copy flags, the labels and the sample flags:









Column
Meaning




DocID
One registrant’s copy of an Exhibit 10 attachment: the registrant’s CIK and a hash of the attachment, joined by a hyphen. Unique in this table and the key every other table joins on.


HashDocument
Hash of the attachment’s content. Shared by all registrant copies of one document, so it groups the copies of one contract.


HashIndex
The filing that carried the attachment. Joins to Summaries (the filing’s announcement) and CtoOrders.


CIK
The registrant’s Central Index Key on EDGAR. With DateFiled, the key for matching other databases.


UrlDocument
Address of the attachment on EDGAR.


FormType
The form the attachment was filed with: 8-K, 10-K, 10-Q, S-1 and so on.


DateFiled
The day EDGAR accepted the filing.


Removed
TRUE where the attachment failed the screen for usable text (reason in RemClass). These attachments stay in the table, flagged, so that what was set aside remains visible.


RemClass
Why the attachment was set aside: too short, not prose, mostly digits, or no readable text.


MultFiler
1 where the filing names more than one registrant, so that the attachment appears once per registrant.


PrimaryFiler
1 on the one copy of each attachment the entity variables were computed from; the other copies carry the same values. Count contracts on PrimaryFiler == 1.


DescSample
1 where the attachment is in the paper’s descriptive sample.


EstiSample
1 where the attachment is in the paper’s estimation sample, which requires a Compustat match on CIK and filing date. The matched Compustat data are not published.


Class
Contract type, twelve categories: the label the paper uses.


ClassRollup
Broad contract type, seven categories: the broad category of Class, as the paper uses it. The part of Class before the colon; Customer / Supplier and R&D roll up to Purchases and Sales; Leases, Licenses and Other stand alone.


ClassBroad
Broad contract type from the additional broad classifier (see BertClassBroad). Where it differs from ClassRollup, HierConsistent is FALSE.


AmendType
Original or Amended: the label the paper uses.





EstiSample marks the paper’s estimation sample, which requires a Compustat match; Compustat is not published (what needs WRDS).


Summaries
One row per current report (Form 8-K or 8-K/A) with an Item 1.01 text announcing a material agreement: 278,997 rows. SumAttached is 1 where the filing carried an Exhibit 10 and 0 where the agreement was announced without the contract. The sample holds the 59 announcements that carried a sampled contract.









Column
Meaning




HashIndex
The 8-K filing. Joins to Contracts where the filing carried a contract.


DocID
The 8-K document the Item 1.01 text was read from; its text is in text/8k or text/8ka.


DateFiled
The day EDGAR accepted the filing.


SumAttached
1 where the filing carried an Exhibit 10; 0 where the agreement was announced without the contract.


SumDates
Distinct agreement dates at the start of the Item 1.01 text: a proxy for the number of agreements announced.


SumDateFirst
The first of those dates: the agreement date.


SumLagDays
DateFiled minus SumDateFirst, in calendar days; negative where the filing precedes the date. Item 1.01 allows four business days.


SumWords
Words in the Item 1.01 text, without its heading and title.


SumBoiler
Share of the text’s four-word phrases that occur in the filings of at least one in a hundred distinct filers (after Lang and Stice-Lawrence 2015).







Places
One row per contract, geographic level (country, state, county or city) with its state and country, party role and law-clause flag, with the number of mentions: 9,545,088 rows, 1,862 in the sample. The table does not name cities or counties; spans/places_geo.parquet (GeoUnit) names them. GeoCountry keeps the country’s name as found in the text, so one country can take several rows in a contract; count countries on GeoCountryIso. Like TermDocs below, the table holds the primary copy of each attachment (PrimaryFiler == 1); HashDocument reaches every registrant copy.









Column
Meaning




DocID
The contract (its primary copy). Joins to Contracts on DocID.


HashDocument
The attachment; joins to every registrant copy in Contracts.


GeoLevel
What the place name resolved to: Country, State, County or City.


GeoState
The US state, where the place gives one.


GeoCountryIso
ISO 3166 alpha-3 country code; USA for US places. Count countries on this column.


GeoCountry
The country’s name as found in the text. One country can appear under several spellings, including other languages.


PartyRole
The party the place was attached to: registrant, cofiler, counterparty, signatory, other, or none.


InLawClause
1 where the place sits in a governing-law clause, so it is a jurisdiction rather than a location.


nMentions
How often the contract mentions this place in this role.







TermDocs
One row per contract and term family, 5 families, on the primary copy of the contract: 5,949,025 rows, 930 in the sample. HashDocument reaches the other registrant copies.









Column
Meaning




DocID
The contract (its primary copy). Joins to Contracts on DocID.


HashDocument
The attachment; joins to every registrant copy in Contracts.


Family
The term family searched for: Pandemic, Disruption, RateReform, Regulation or Boilerplate.


nHits
Occurrences of any term of the family; a term found twice counts twice.


nTerms
Distinct terms of the family found.


HasTerm
1 where nHits is positive.


FirstPos
Relative position of the first hit: 0 at the start of the text, 1 at its end.


PerKWords
nHits per thousand words of the contract.







CtoOrders
One row per exhibit reference in a confidential treatment order, whatever the order decided (Status) and whether or not it was linked to a contract (LinkStatus): 32,410 rows. The sample holds the 17 references linked to a sampled contract.









Column
Meaning




OrderDocID
The order’s own document on EDGAR; its text is in text/cto.


OrderDate
The day the order was filed.


Status
GRANTING, DENYING or REVOKING, as the order’s title states.


IsExtension
1 where the order extends an earlier grant.


ExhibitNo
The exhibit number the order names, such as 10.1.


ReleaseDate
When the granted treatment ends.


DocID
The contract the reference was resolved to. Joins to Contracts on DocID.


LinkStatus
A-linked where the order was linked to a contract; otherwise the numbered step at which linking failed (1 no reference read, 2 not an Exhibit 10, 3 source filing not named, 4 filing not on EDGAR, 5 filing ambiguous, 6 no exhibit retrieved from that filing, 7 exhibit ambiguous, 8 lettered exhibit number, 9 exhibit not among those retrieved).







The contract index, the labelled sample and the keyword terms
ContractIndex.csv.gz locates each contract on EDGAR, keyed on DocID: the filing (AccessionNumber, CIK, CompanyName, FormType, DateFiled), the attachment within it (DocName, DocSeq, DocDesc), its labels and the two EDGAR links; its codebook below lists every column. It is a compressed CSV, so it opens without a parquet reader.
Labels.parquet is the labelled sample: one row per labelled contract with the annotators’ labels and the cross-validation fold in which it was held out (Fold), 4,398 rows, of which the sample holds 180.
KeywordTerms.parquet holds the keyword terms of all three classification tasks, 160 rows, with Task naming the task a term belongs to. It is described with the keyword classifier.

section: Three things to know before counting
text:
Three things to know before counting
The examples below start from the contracts table of the sample:

contracts <- arrow::read_parquet("sample/core/Contracts.parquet")  # core/Contracts.parquet in the package


The unit of observation is the registrant copy
One row of the contracts table is one registrant’s copy of one Exhibit 10 attachment. When a filing names two registrants, the same attachment arrives twice, once under each registrant’s CIK. HashDocument identifies the attachment itself and is shared by its copies; DocID identifies the copy. DocID is the registrant’s CIK and the hash of the attachment joined by a hyphen, as the check below confirms; the accession number sits in UrlIndexPage and, under its own name, in the contract index.

contracts |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Rows = dplyr::n(),                              # copies in the sample
    Attachments = dplyr::n_distinct(HashDocument),  # distinct documents among them
    DocIDIsCikAndHash = all(  # TRUE when every key is the CIK and the hash, not the accession number
      DocID == paste(
        CIK,           # the registrant
        HashDocument,  # the attachment
        sep = "-"      # joined as in the published key
      )
    )
  )

That is 28 of the 214 rows dropped as further copies of an attachment already counted.


Rejected attachments stay in the file
Removed marks an attachment that failed the screen for usable text, and RemClass gives the reason. These attachments stay in the table, flagged, so that what was set aside remains visible; an analysis that wants readable contracts filters on Removed.

contracts |>
  dplyr::count(
    Removed,  # TRUE where the attachment failed the screen for usable text

The two filters together leave 183 of the 214 rows of the sample: one readable contract each.


Span offsets are 0-based and half-open
Every span file locates its entity with a start and a stop offset into the published text of the document. The offsets are 0-based and half-open, and they count characters, not bytes. In R the span is stringi::stri_sub(TextRaw, Start + 1, Stop); in Python it is text[Start:Stop].

options(arrow.use_altrep = FALSE)  # plain R strings, so a text joined to many spans is not converted for each
text <- arrow::read_parquet("sample/text/exhibit10/exhibit10_sample.parquet")
dates <- arrow::read_parquet("sample/spans/date_spans.parquet")

    text,         # the published text the offsets point into
    by = "DocID"  # a span file and the text share the document key

    DocID,                       # the document
    DateStart,                   # 0-based start
    DateStop,                    # half-open stop
    Sliced = stringi::stri_sub(  # what the offsets cut out of the text
      TextRaw,                   # the published text of the document
      DateStart + 1,             # a 0-based start is R's 1-based first character
      DateStop                   # a half-open stop is R's inclusive last character
    ),
    DateText                     # what the span file stores

The same holds for every span file. Each names its offsets after its entity (DateStart, MentionStart, …) and most store the text they found beside them; the governing-law file stores none.

offset_check <- function(file) {
  spans <- arrow::read_parquet(file) |>
    dplyr::inner_join(
      text,         # the published text the offsets point into
      by = "DocID"  # a span file and the text share the document key
    )
  start <- grep(
    "Start$",      # the first ...Start column is the span's own start
    names(spans),  # the columns of this span file
    value = TRUE   # the name rather than its position
  )[1]
  end <- sub(
    "Start$",  # DateStart, MentionStart, ...
    "Stop",    # ... pair with DateStop, MentionStop, ...
    start      # the start column found above
  )
  stored <- grep(
    "Text$",       # DateText, PlaceText, SpanText, ...: the text the extractor stored
    names(spans),  # the columns of this span file
    value = TRUE   # the name rather than its position
  )[1]
  sliced <- stringi::stri_sub(
    spans$TextRaw,       # the published text of each span's document
    spans[[start]] + 1,  # 0-based start to R's 1-based first character
    spans[[end]]         # half-open stop is R's inclusive last character
  )
  tibble::tibble(
    File = basename(file),                    # the span file
    Rows = nrow(spans),                       # rows in the sample
    WithOffsets = sum(!is.na(sliced)),        # rows that locate a span
    Stored = stored,                          # the column holding the stored text, if any
    SliceEqualsStored = if (is.na(stored)) {  # spans whose slice is the stored text
      NA_integer_
    } else {
      sum(
        sliced == spans[[stored]],  # slice and stored text agree
        na.rm = TRUE                # a row without offsets has nothing to compare
      )
    }
  )
}

list.files(
  "sample/spans",           # every span file of the sample
  pattern = "\\.parquet$",  # the codebook beside them is not a span file
  full.names = TRUE         # read_parquet needs the path, not the name
) |>
  lapply(offset_check) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows()

Counting characters matters. Curly quotes, section signs and bullets take more than one byte each, and a tool that slices bytes cuts the wrong text for every span after the first of them:

first_wide <- text |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    DocID,                                         # the document
    FirstWide = stringi::stri_locate_first_regex(  # where byte and character positions first part
      TextRaw,                                     # the published text
      "[^\\u0000-\\u007f]"                         # the first character outside ASCII
    )[, "start"]
  )

dates |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    first_wide,   # each document's first character outside ASCII
    by = "DocID"  # one position per document
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Spans = dplyr::n(),        # date spans in the sample
    AfterWideCharacter = sum(  # spans a tool that slices bytes would cut wrongly
      DateStart >= FirstWide,  # the span starts after a character of more than one byte
      na.rm = TRUE             # a document without such a character shifts nothing
    )
  )

In Python the slice is the same once the text is a str. PlaceStart and LawStart are stored as doubles, and pandas reads the offsets of org_mentions as floats because its rows without a span have none; dropping those rows and casting with int() makes the block work on every span file:
import pandas as pd

text = pd.read_parquet("sample/text/exhibit10/exhibit10_sample.parquet").set_index("DocID")["TextRaw"]
dates = pd.read_parquet("sample/spans/date_spans.parquet").dropna(subset=["DateStart"])

dates["Sliced"] = [
    text[doc][int(start):int(stop)]  # 0-based and half-open: Python's own slice
    for doc, start, stop in zip(
        dates["DocID"],       # the document
        dates["DateStart"],   # 0-based start
        dates["DateStop"],    # half-open stop
    )
]

title: The data
text:
Known issues
The package’s README describes these issues of v1.0.0; the figures come from the sample.

Columbia. The gazetteer reads “Columbia” as the country Colombia, so Colombia is heavily over-counted in Places, places_geo and the country counts of Contracts; in US contracts the word is almost always the District of Columbia, British Columbia or a US city. In the sample, 25 rows of places_geo read “Columbia” as Colombia.
Country spellings. A country can appear under several names, some in other languages; count on GeoCountryIso. In the Places table of the sample, USA appears as “United States”, “United States Of America”, “Usa”.
Durations. DurationYears is left missing above 30 years (DurationDropped says so); other date columns are not capped.
Broad label. The paper’s broad category is ClassRollup. ClassBroad comes from an additional model trained on the broad labels directly; HierConsistent marks where the two differ (classification).
Span offsets. LawStart and PlaceStart are stored as whole-numbered doubles, the other offsets as integers.
Parties. A contract without any identified organisation has one row in org_mentions without a span (above).
No document-level gold set exists for the entities. The labelled sample in Labels.parquet covers the classification, not the extraction.
The text as read. TextRaw is exactly the text the classifiers and extractors read. In some HTML documents, quotation marks, apostrophes and dashes appear as control characters (U+0080 to U+009F): they were written in Windows-1252 and read as Latin-1. The package’s README gives a repair in R and in Python that swaps one character for one, so every offset stays valid. A model or extractor run on repaired text reads slightly different input from the one that produced the data.


Not in the package

Compustat. It is licensed. EstiSample marks the rows of the paper’s estimation sample; the match to Compustat can be rebuilt from CIK and DateFiled (what needs WRDS).
Amounts. Monetary amounts were extracted but are not used by the paper and are not published.

title: The data
text:
Licences
The tables, the span files and the other data of the package are published under CC BY 4.0. The fine-tuned classifiers are published under CC BY-SA 4.0, the licence of the model they were trained from. The documents in the documents part are filings the SEC made public on EDGAR. The extraction image contains LexNLP, which is licensed under the AGPL-3.0, and carries a notice (lexnlp/NOTICE.md). The full texts of the licences are in the LICENSES folder of the site’s repository.

title: Stata
text: The paper’s regressions and several of its tables and figures are estimated in Stata. The do-files will be published on this page once they are cleaned up. They read a Stata copy of the contracts table of the database and Compustat data from WRDS, which are licensed and not published (what needs WRDS).

title: Stata
text:
Reading the tables
The tables of the database are parquet files, and no .dta files are published. Stata reads a table once it has been converted with R or Python; the codebooks give each column’s name in Stata (StataName).

title: Stata
text:
Slicing a span
Span offsets count characters from 0, the end exclusive (span offsets). Stata’s usubstr() counts characters where substr() counts bytes, so a span is sliced with usubstr(). For the date spans, with each span’s document text, TextRaw, merged on DocID:
generate DateSlice = usubstr( ///
  TextRaw,                    /// the document's text, as every offset reads it
  DateStart + 1,              /// Stata counts from 1, the offsets from 0
  DateStop - DateStart        /// a length in characters, not an end
)
